I feature here how I explained multiple testing, False Discovery Rate (FDR) control and the problem of p-values miscalibration — concepts they frequently encounter in practice but often find unclear or intimidating.

<div class="card card-retractable" style="margin-bottom: 2rem;" onclick="this.classList.toggle('expanded')">

  <p style="text-align: center;font-weight: bold; font-size: 28px;">
  Challenges
  </p>
   Nowadays, **biological experiments often go hand in hand with high throughput and big data, providing the opportunity to test numerous hypotheses**. This complexifies the statistical data analysis, and requires **extra level of caution**. While experimentalists are often aware of it: 

  - the topic of multiple testing is mathematically abstract and often perceived as difficult, obscur and/or inaccessible;
  - experimentalists have highly heterogeneous statistical backgrounds (from minimal to solid knowledge). <br>
  
  The goal of these workshops was not just explanation, but:
  
  - building **intuition and confidence**;
  - showcasing what breaks in multiple vs simple hypothesis testing;
  - enabling participants to engage with these concepts independently after the session.
  </div>

<div class="card-row">
  
  <div class="card card-retractable" onclick="this.classList.toggle('expanded')">
  <p style="text-align: center;font-weight: bold; font-size: 28px;">
  Approach
  </p>

  I structured the workshop around progressive intuition-building, grounded in familiar visual tools.

  Key elements:

  - starting from a simple, **concrete example to introduce the problem**;
  - using histograms as a central visual language, **leveraging familiar representations**;
  - guiding participants through **logical reasoning steps**:
    - why multiple testing inflates false positives;
    - what p-value miscalibration means in practice;
  - introducing **formulas without avoiding them**, but supporting them with:
    - color coding
    - visual representations
    - intuitive interpretation

  </div>

  <div class="card card-retractable" onclick="this.classList.toggle('expanded')">
  <p style="text-align: center;font-weight: bold; font-size: 28px;">
  Strengths
  </p>
  - Design of **structured learning experiences under time constraints** (1h workshops);
  - ability to make **abstract statistical concepts intuitive and non-intimidating**;
  - **adaptation to audiences** with diverse levels of confidence in mathematics;
  - use of **visual tools** (histograms, color, diagrams) to support conceptual understanding;
  - **connecting theory to real-world** data analysis practice.
  </div>
</div>

<div class="card card-retractable" style="margin-bottom: 2rem;" onclick="this.classList.toggle('expanded')">
  <p style="text-align: center;font-weight: bold; font-size: 28px;">
  Impact
  </p>
  **Why do we need experimentalists to build intuition and understanding based on theory?** <br>
  <i>A fish to a man, you feed him for a day, teach him to fish, he will feed for a lifetime.</i> <br> <br>
  Incomprehension of statistical concepts often lead experimentalists to mistrust - or blindly trust! - data analysts. While the former can cause incorrect data analysis, the second leads to strong dependency. <br>
  Explaining fundamental statistical concepts with intuition while keeping rigor is key to enabling interactions and constructive collaborations between experimentalists and data analysts. Inter-disciplinary collaboration performs better when both sides understands each other - and can thus reasonably rely on each other expertise to go further and deeper.
</div>
